text: CFTC Chair Cites BTC, ETH, SOL, XLM, XTZ and XRP as Examples of Digital Commodities CFTC Chair Michael Selig provided further details on the previously announced Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM framework. The proposed rules would generally require covered retail crypto transactions to be intermediated by futures commission merchants (FCMs) and impose requirements related to customer asset segregation, capital, anti-money laundering and proof of reserves. For onchain transactions, the CFTC is proposing to clarify that delivery of crypto assets to a user's external, non-custodial wallet within 28 days would generally satisfy the "actual delivery" exception. Selig said the CFTC is also exploring a durable regulatory policy for developers who only publish software without soliciting or taking orders, controlling execution or holding customer assets. He also cited the CFTC and SEC's joint crypto asset taxonomy, which lists BTC, ETH, SOL, XLM, XTZ and XRP as examples of "digital commodities." — link

text: FinCEN withdraws 2020 unhosted crypto wallet rule, takes no further action The U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has withdrawn a 2020 proposal that would have imposed reporting and recordkeeping requirements on certain transactions involving unhosted crypto wallets, saying it will take no further action on the proposal. The rule would have required banks and money services businesses (MSBs) to report transactions exceeding $10,000 involving unhosted or certain covered wallets and verify customer identities, while transactions above $3,000 would have been subject to recordkeeping requirements. FinCEN said the withdrawal is part of the Trump administration's efforts to ensure digital asset regulations are "fit-for-purpose." FinCEN announced the withdrawal of two proposed digital asset rules. One would have imposed recordkeeping, identity verification and reporting requirements on certain transactions involving convertible virtual currencies (CVCs) and unhosted wallets; the other would have designated convertible virtual currency mixing as a class of transactions of primary money laundering concern and imposed a special measure. FinCEN said it withdrew the proposals after considering public comments, as part of the Trump administration's deregulatory agenda and efforts to make digital asset regulations fit for purpose. — link

text: Hyperliquid receives first $14.58M USDC payment under AQAv2 for HYPE buybacks Hyperliquid received its first $14.58 million USDC payment under the AQAv2 framework, adding a funding source for HYPE buybacks beyond trading fees. Under the mechanism, roughly 90% of cost-adjusted reserve yield generated on USDC supply is shared with the protocol and routed to the Assistance Fund, which purchases HYPE. The first payment covered a 30-day period. — link

text: Good entry on $CODEC here Had some issues with the Machine Fun launch as the fee mechanism had to be reconfigured due to Raydiums infra not being able to do the specific parameters they wanted. Which led to a sell off alongside an overall pullback with onchain the past week. I purposely haven't spoken much about what they're building or explained how they fit into architectures of foundational models. Since I've been waiting for Machine Fun to go live, to be a direct funnel for attention and attracting builders + traders. We've had such a strong focus on memes, as consensus turned to software being solved thanks to AI's advancements. But with any innovation, there's always another side to the coin. What are the ramifications to adjacent sectors like physical hardware and robotics when the marginal cost of cognitive and digital execution drops to zero? At this point in the cycle, BTC's clearly broken structure, memes have been dominating the past few months and we're yet to see a real utility meta. What Codec and Machine Fun are looking to do hasn't been done before. It's converging permissionless fund raising, robotics and speculation all in one. The simulation tooling (SimArena) they're building can't be vamped as it requires large amounts of personal testing from physics engines and real world deployments. As these physics engines inside foundational models become more accurate, then robotics slowly converges on becoming a compute problem as tooling becomes advanced enough to brute force real world scenarios. Simulations in turn become significantly more valuable. This is a key component as the launchpad will act as a bootstrapping funnel to acquire more devs/users to use SimArena and grow the available public modules/packages/libraries. While the launchpad itself will attract tons of solo/small teams of developers who like Codec in the early days, were looking for ways to scale their robots, physical hardware, electronics, software etc. Which will all flywheel into the native token plus having sustainable and transparent unlocks for founders, so traders can accurately see circulating supply and unlock schedules + distribution. Considering what they've been building for over a year and the network they've built, I still think it's extremely cheap at 8 mil granted how much robotics has and is going to grow. We aren't far away from significant breakthroughs and robotics having it's chatgpt moment if you pay attention to development by leading foundations.
